role: builder — the data loader had no retry; a 503 on any of 569 files killed boot and was reported as 'A file the game needs is missing'
headline: The loader now retries 5xx/408/429 and network errors with bounded backoff, NEVER retries a 404, and every failure names the status, the URL and the attempt count. tools/playability/loader-retry.mjs --self-test is the instrument: 8/8 arms, including a delete-the-fix null control, a control-sanity arm, and two sabotages that force the checks to go red for the wrong behaviour.

what_changed.game/src/engine.js: loadData()/fetchJson rewritten as a bounded retry ladder. LOAD_RETRY = 4 attempts, backoff 250/750/1750 ms with +-40% jitter, whole-load sleep budget 12000 ms, whole-load ceiling 24 retries. CAP ON ADDED BOOT LATENCY: at most 12 s of sleeping across the entire load plus the round-trip cost of at most 24 extra requests; a healthy boot sleeps zero. Retryable = status >= 500, 408, 429, or fetch rejecting (network/TLS). Everything else, 404 above all, fails on the first response. Deliberately NO per-request timeout — a 17 MB world on a slow phone is a long healthy download and a timeout tuned here would abort it; that leaves a genuinely hung socket hanging, as before, and the comment says so rather than pretending otherwise. Every attempt/wait/recovery is recorded on globalThis.__ES_LOAD_RETRIES so the retry is watchable from Node, from the boot notice and from a bug report.
what_changed.game/index.html: the boot notice no longer calls a 5xx a missing file. 5xx/408/429 report as weather in the progress line ('The server refused N requests (503 on ...). Nothing is missing — the game is asking again.') and set window.__BOOT_TRANSIENT; anything else stays loud immediately with the device line. When the retries are exhausted the loader's rejection lands on the glass through the existing ready() path, carrying the status, the URL and the attempt count, and the notice does not hide. deviceLine() gained a 'load' field summarising __ES_LOAD_RETRIES (requests, retries, ms waiting, where it gave up, last status+file).
what_changed.tools/playability/loader-retry.mjs: NEW. A fault-injecting static server over the real repo plus real Chromium. --self-test runs all eight arms in one line. Exports deleteTheFix/sabotageRetry404/sabotageNoticeLie so a successor can reuse the controls.

found_while_building: The instrument-lie arm first went red for the WRONG reason — arm 2's checks ran in an order that tripped the transient-count assertion before the truthfulness assertion, so the sabotage proved only that something changed. That is the shape rule 6 warns about (a control that looks like a result). Arm 2's checks were reordered to put the two lie assertions first and the sabotage now bites the intended check by name; both instrument arms assert WHICH check went red, not merely that one did.
aggregation: node tools/harness/boot-check.mjs PASS. node tools/harness/lint-determinism.mjs 0 errors, 5 informational (the new Math.random for jitter is one of them, on a non-simulation path — it runs before installGuards() and nothing it produces can reach a traced value).
contention: node tools/contention.mjs --gate returned exit 3 (load 4.0-4.8 per core, 2-3 browser instances) before every browser run here. I proceeded, per rule 21's escape clause, and am saying so: this measures boot-time correctness, not timing or pixels. Every assertion is a request count, a status code or a string; the only contention-sensitive number in the report is elapsed_ms and nothing is asserted on it.
could_not_do: This was measured against a LOCAL fault server, not against GitHub Pages. Chromium in this container cannot TLS-handshake through the egress proxy (see orchestration/status/PLAYABILITY.json, constraint_item_1), so no browser here can reach the live host. The retry ladder is therefore proven against a server that behaves like Pages' CDN on the axis that matters (status codes and their timing) and not against Pages itself. The standing playability agent's next live run is what closes that gap.

No per-request timeout was added, so a socket that accepts the connection and never answers still hangs the boot for ever. That is a real remaining defect of the same family; it is named in the engine.js comment rather than quietly fixed, because any timeout short enough to help here is short enough to abort a legitimate slow download on the device this whole piece is written for.
The 429 path is retried on the same ladder as 5xx and ignores Retry-After. Pages does not rate-limit static assets in practice, so this is untested rather than wrong.
next_step: none — piece complete. A critic should attack the instrument first: the honest attack is whether the two sabotage arms could pass while the underlying checks are inert, and whether a 4-attempt ladder is enough for the failure Pages actually produces.
